extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, comedy writers, and theatre students learning to write or evaluate farce
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for creating or judging theatrical farce — a stage comedy relying on exaggerated, improbable situations, rapid escalation, physical business, and tightly staged entrances/exits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly improbable situations
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of comedy that relies on exaggerated, improbable, or ridiculous situations; Is the situation highly improbable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farce is built on situations that stretch plausibility. The central circumstance should feel ludicrous or unlikely enough to drive comedic complication rather than realistic cause-and-effect. (Page definition: 'Comic dramatic piece using highly improbable situations...')

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid/continuous escalation of complications
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapidly escalating complications; The plot escalates continuously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complications should mount quickly and without long pauses, each new development raising confusion and urgency. Ray Cooney's rule emphasizes continuous escalation as structural engine of farce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breathless pace
rubrics_metrics.description: Breathless pace; Is the pace breathless?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing and momentum are essential — scenes should move quickly with little downtime between beats. A breathless tempo keeps misunderstandings and physical business feeling urgent and funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Often ends with everything resolved comically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite the chaos, farces typically close with a satisfying, tidy reveal or reconciliation that pays off the layered confusions. The final reveal should deliver payoff for the accumulated misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotyped, exaggerated, one-dimensional characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotyped, one-dimensional figures; Driven by exaggeration; Vehicles for comedic situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters are often broad, easily recognizable types whose exaggerated traits generate predictable, overblown reactions. They function primarily to create and sustain comic complications rather than deep psychological arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters in over their heads
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protagonists (and ensemble) should be outmatched by the situations they face, producing frantic attempts to cope that escalate the comedy. This is a key emotional state that fuels farce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic irony / audience knows more than characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the audience know more than the characters (dramatic irony)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farce depends on the audience being aware of misunderstandings the characters are not. This dramatic irony creates tension and humor as viewers anticipate collisions and reveals. (From 'Why Farce Is Funny': 'Audience sees the misunderstandings the characters can't.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Single, precise setting / shared physical space
rubrics_metrics.description: Most action takes place in one precise location; Same physical space for all characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confining action to a single, well-defined space concentrates physical comedy and heightens the impact of entrances/exits, doors, and overlapping business. Staging economy is typical of classic farce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifting relationships and rising stakes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpersonal dynamics should change rapidly as complications unfold, with stakes escalating (socially or personally) to increase urgency and comedic risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakes feel life-or-death to characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The stakes must feel life-or-death to the characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters must perceive their dilemmas as existentially important even when the audience sees them as trivial; this mismatch amplifies desperation and comic behavior (Ray Cooney rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrances and exits must matter
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entrances and exits are structural beats that trigger complications, misunderstandings, and reversals. Timing and purposefulness of each doorway moment are crucial to the farce's machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information withholding and misunderstandings
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters never share information except by misunderstanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key information should be withheld, misheard, or misinterpreted so that characters act on false premises; direct transmission of facts between characters undermines farce. This creates sustained dramatic irony and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doors as active stage elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Doors are characters in their own right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical set pieces (especially doors) are integral comic tools: they conceal, reveal, separate and reunite characters. Use doors for slams, near-misses, hiding, and timed entrances to produce laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threatened violence over performed violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Violence must be threatened more than performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threats and the suggestion of force heighten stakes and panic without resorting to real harm; implied violence fuels frantic action while keeping tone comic (Ray Cooney rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical comedy and business (pratfalls, stunts, clowning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pratfalls, spit-takes, stunts, clowning; Actions more important than words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physicality is central: visual gags, pratfalls, and stunts often drive the humor more than dialogue. Choreograph physical business carefully and prioritize clear, repeatable beats that read to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound tension through repeated misses and layered confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated misses generate compound tension; Final reveal pays off layered confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sequences of near-misses and escalating misunderstandings so that each failure compounds prior complications, creating cumulative comic pressure resolved by a final reveal or reconciliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples & traditions as models
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical and modern exemplars: Plautus, Molière; Feydeau (French farce); A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum; Noises Off; Fawlty Towers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study these examples for structure, timing, character types, and the interplay of physical and verbal comedy. They illustrate how the conventions above are put into practice.
